content.title: About
content.content: Bagel with wheat bran is a whole‑grain bakery product made from wheat flour, wheat bran and yeast. The bran gives it a nutty aroma, a dense crumb and a higher fiber content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wheat bran is the outer layer of the grain, rich in fiber, B‑vitamins and minerals.
Bagels are traditionally shaped as a ring; adding bran makes them more nutritious without losing shape.
Bran can help lower blood glucose by slowing carbohydrate absorption.
In some countries bagels with bran are served for breakfast with cottage cheese or yogurt.
Wheat bran is often used in diet plans for weight control.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Bran provides soluble and insoluble fiber that supports healthy digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains thiamine, niacin and folate, which are essential for energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Rich in magnesium, iron and zinc, supporting muscle function and immune health.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The high fiber content causes a slower rise in blood sugar after eating.

items.title: Cardiovascular support
items.content: Fiber helps lower LDL (bad) cholesterol levels.

items.title: Wheat allergy or gluten intolerance
items.content: People with wheat allergy or celiac disease should avoid this product.

items.title: High fiber load
items.content: Excessive bran intake may cause bloating, gas or diarrhea.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytates can reduce the absorption of certain minerals if consumed in large amounts.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The bagel can be eaten plain as a snack, sliced and topped with cream cheese, avocado, smoked salmon, or used for open‑face sandwiches. Light toasting enhances texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep bagels in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage refrigerate (up to 7 days) or freeze (up to 3 months).

content.title: About
content.content: Cooked celery consists of stalks that have been peeled and boiled until tender. The cooking process softens the texture while preserving its distinctive aroma, making it easy to digest. It is used in soups, stews, salads, and as a side dish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Celery belongs to the Apiaceae family and is closely related to parsley and dill.
Celery was known in ancient Egypt, where it was used for medicinal purposes.
Celery contains phthalides, compounds responsible for its characteristic scent.
In many cuisines, cooked celery is often served with a cream or sour cream sauce.
Celery can be grown as an annual or a perennial plant.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, helps regulate blood sugar levels, and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low-calorie food
items.content: 100 g of cooked celery provides about 16 kcal, making it an excellent choice for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamin B6, folate, and niacin aid metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Source of potassium and sodium
items.content: These minerals help maintain fluid balance and blood pressure.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavonoids and vitamin C protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to celery, ranging from skin rashes to swelling.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Celery can enhance the effects of certain anticoagulants; consult a healthcare professional if you take such medication.

items.title: Oxalates
items.content: Oxalate content may contribute to kidney stone formation in susceptible persons.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked celery can be served as a standalone side, added to soups, stews, vegetable casseroles, or diced into salads. It pairs well with lemon juice, olive oil, and soft cheeses.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked celery in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3–4 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions after cooling.

egg-substitute-omelet-scrambled-or-fried.title: Egg substitute, omelet, scrambled, or fried, with cheese

content.title: About
content.content: Egg substitute is a ready‑made blend that allows you to make an omelet, scrambled eggs or fried dishes without using real eggs. The formula typically contains plant proteins, starch, flavorings and sometimes additives that mimic the yolk. When cooked with cheese, the result is a tender, flavorful dish suitable for vegetarians and those with egg allergies.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Egg substitute is a staple in vegan cooking for achieving an egg‑like texture.
The mix often includes turmeric or natural coloring to give a yellow hue similar to yolk.
Some brands add probiotics to improve gut health.
It is sold dry and has a long shelf life, making it convenient for pantry storage.
When combined with cheese, the substitute binds moisture and creates a creamy mouthfeel.

items.title: Low cholesterol
items.content: Unlike real eggs, the substitute contains no cholesterol, which is beneficial for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Typical blends provide 10–15 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Added probiotics and dietary fiber can promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Allergy‑friendly
items.content: Absence of egg proteins makes it safe for people with egg allergies.

items.title: Vitamin B12 fortification
items.content: Many versions are fortified with B12, helping vegans meet their daily requirement.

items.title: Soy protein allergy
items.content: Many substitutes are soy‑based; individuals allergic to soy should avoid them.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some products contain added salt, so those monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

items.title: Processed ingredients
items.content: The blend may include artificial flavors and preservatives that are not suitable for everyone.

items.title: Missing nutrients
items.content: Unlike eggs, the substitute may lack natural vitamin D and choline.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Mix the powder with water (or plant milk) according to package directions, usually 1 tsp per 60 ml liquid. Cook in a lightly oiled pan, adding grated cheese toward the end so it melts. The mixture works for omelets, scrambled dishes, and fried egg‑style patties.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dry substitute in a sealed container in a cool, dry place. After opening, use within 3–6 months. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or changes color.

muffin-english-wheat-bran-with-raisins.title: Muffin, English, wheat bran, with raisins

content.title: About
content.content: A wheat‑bran muffin with raisins is a baked treat made from whole‑grain wheat bran enriched with sweet raisins. It offers a light crumb, a nutty bran flavor, and natural sweetness from the fruit.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Wheat bran is the outer layer of the grain and is high in dietary fiber and nutrients.
Raisins provide natural sweetness without added refined sugar.
These muffins are a traditional English snack often enjoyed at breakfast or tea time.
Bran improves the texture of the muffin, making it denser and more flavorful.
The combination of bran and raisins makes the product popular among those monitoring blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Bran supplies a substantial amount of dietary fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat bran contains B1, B2, and B6 vitamins important for metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Raisins are a good source of iron, which contributes to hemoglobin formation.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: The blend of bran and raisins leads to a slower rise in blood glucose.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Raisins are rich in polyphenols that help combat oxidative stress.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: People with gluten intolerance or wheat allergy may experience reactions.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Raisins add natural sugars, so individuals with diabetes should watch portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Muffins can be calorie‑dense, so moderation is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the muffin as a snack, split it and spread with cottage cheese, crumble over yogurt, or use as a base for dessert parfaits.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days or refrigerate for up to a week. For longer keeping, freeze in a freezer‑safe bag.

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain frozen pancakes are a ready‑to‑cook product made from whole‑grain flour, eggs, milk and a touch of sugar. They cook quickly on a skillet while retaining the nutritional benefits of whole grains and a pleasant aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain pancakes contain more fiber than traditional white pancakes.
Freezing preserves most B‑vitamins and minerals when the product is properly packaged.
Many brands fortify whole‑grain pancakes with iron and folic acid to boost nutritional value.
In some countries they are sold in single‑serve packets designed for one or two portions.
Pancakes can be cooked without added oil using a non‑stick pan.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain flour provides dietary fiber that supports digestive health and promotes satiety.

items.title: Complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs release energy slowly, helping maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B2 and niacin are involved in energy metabolism and nervous‑system function.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Pancakes supply iron, magnesium and zinc, which are important for blood formation and immunity.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: When cooked without added butter or oil, they remain a low‑calorie option.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Whole‑grain flour contains gluten, making the product unsuitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Some brands add a small amount of sugar; individuals monitoring blood sugar should check the label.

items.title: Possible additives
items.content: Preservatives or stabilizers may be present; those with sensitivities should choose additive‑free versions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Thaw the pancakes in the microwave or at room temperature, then cook on a dry non‑stick skillet 1–2 minutes per side. Serve with berries, yogurt, nut butter or a light syrup.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep frozen pancakes in their original packaging in a freezer at –18 °C. After opening, use within 3–4 days, returning them to a sealed container in the freezer.

content.title: About
content.content: Passion fruit (Passiflora edulis) is a tropical fruit with aromatic sweet‑tart pulp filled with numerous edible seeds. The fruit grows in South America, Africa, Asia and the Caribbean. It is eaten fresh or used in juices, desserts, sauces and marinades.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Passion fruit belongs to the Passifloraceae family and is related to kiwi and pears.
The seeds are rich in dietary fiber and antioxidants.
The dark‑green rind changes color from yellow to purple depending on the variety.
In traditional medicine the fruit is used to aid digestion and reduce anxiety.
Passion fruit juice is a popular ingredient in cocktails, ice cream and meat marinades.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and helps synthesize collagen.

items.title: Contains vitamin A and carotenoids
items.content: These nutrients help maintain healthy vision and skin.

items.title: Good source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes normal digestion and contributes to satiety.

items.title: Antioxidant properties
items.content: Flavonoids and polyphenols protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Potassium and magnesium help regulate blood pressure and support heart function.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience an allergic reaction to passion fruit.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: High acidity can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Seed hardness
items.content: Seeds are hard; they should be ground or avoided for young children to prevent choking.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cut the fruit in half and scoop out the pulp with a spoon. The juice can be added to smoothies, cocktails, sauces and desserts. Seeds can be mixed into yogurt, oatmeal or baked goods for a crunchy texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store passion fruit in the refrigerator’s fruit drawer, where it will keep for up to 2 weeks. Ripe fruits are best used within a few days. Discard any fruit with soft spots or off‑odors.

pasta-whole-grain-with-cream-sauce-and-m.title: Whole Grain Pasta with Cream Sauce and Meat

content.title: About
content.content: Whole grain pasta with cream sauce and meat is a dish that combines whole‑grain pasta, a smooth cream sauce, and tender pieces of stewed meat. The whole‑grain pasta retains bran and germ, making it more nutritious, while the cream sauce adds a rich, velvety texture and mild flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain pasta provides more fiber and micronutrients than traditional white pasta.
Cream sauces are typically made from cream, butter, and seasonings, giving them a higher calorie count but a luxurious taste.
The meat component can be beef, pork, or chicken, each imparting its own distinct flavor profile.
Pasta is traditionally cooked al dente to preserve bite and lower the glycemic index.
In Italy, similar dishes are sometimes baked as "pasta al forno".

items.title: Rich in fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta contains both soluble and insoluble fiber, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Complex carbohydrates provide sustained energy and help maintain satiety.

items.title: Meat‑derived protein
items.content: Meat adds complete protein essential for tissue repair and muscle maintenance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole‑grain flour and meat are good sources of B1, B3, and B6 vitamins, which play key roles in metabolism.

items.title: Calcium and vitamin D from cream
items.content: The cream sauce supplies calcium and vitamin D, supporting bone health.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: The cream sauce and meat make the dish calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight management.

items.title: Saturated fat
items.content: Cream and butter contain saturated fats, which can affect cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Dairy allergy or lactose intolerance
items.content: People with dairy sensitivities should use alternative sauces.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared sauces often contain salt; those monitoring sodium intake may want to reduce added salt.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, tossed with the sauce and meat. Garnish with fresh herbs, grated Parmesan, or vegetables for added flavor and texture.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. The cream sauce may separate; gently reheat and stir before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Fresh potato hash brown are made from boiled potatoes that are shredded, formed into small patties and fried until golden and crisp. They have a mild potato flavor, a crunchy outer crust and a soft interior. Hash browns are commonly served as a side dish for breakfast, lunch or dinner.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Traditionally hash brown are made from raw grated potato, but the fresh version uses cooked potato for a softer interior.
In the United States hash brown are a staple in fast‑food restaurants and school cafeterias.
They can be flavored with onion, herbs or cheese to vary the taste.
Hash brown are believed to have originated in the early 20th century as a way to use leftover boiled potatoes.
In some countries they are served with sour cream or yogurt dip.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Potatoes provide complex carbohydrates that supply sustained energy.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Fresh potatoes contain vitamin C, which supports the immune system and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports normal heart function.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Hash browns retain dietary fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Low fat when prepared properly
items.content: If cooked with minimal oil or baked, they can be a moderately low‑calorie option.

items.title: Potato allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to potatoes.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: When fried, salt is often added; excessive sodium intake can raise blood pressure.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: High‑temperature frying can produce acrylamide, a potential toxin; moderate heat or baking is recommended.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes have a high glycemic index, which can cause rapid blood sugar spikes in diabetics.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Hash browns can be enjoyed as a snack, served alongside eggs, omelets, salads, or used in burgers. They reheat well in the oven or skillet to restore crispness. Garnish with fresh herbs and serve with sour cream or yogurt dip if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked hash browns in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze them in a separate bag; reheating in the oven will keep the crust crispy.

content.title: About
content.content: White sauce (béchamel) and gravy are classic culinary foundations used in European and Russian cuisines. Béchamel is made from butter, flour and milk, while gravy may include stock, cream and aromatic additions. Both sauces give dishes a delicate flavor, creamy texture and help bind ingredients together.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Béchamel is one of the five “mother” sauces of French cuisine, based on a roux.
The name “béchamel” comes from Louis de Béchamel, a favorite of King Louis XIV of France.
In Russian cuisine, gravy is often prepared from meat or vegetable stock and thickened with flour or starch.
Cream sauces can be flavored with herbs, cheese, mustard or spices, making them very versatile.
Béchamel is commonly used in lasagna, moussaka, casseroles and as a creamy topping for fish.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Milk in the sauce provides calcium, essential for bones and teeth.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Milk and cream contain vitamin B2 (riboflavin) and B12, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains protein
items.content: Dairy components add a modest amount of complete protein.

items.title: Improves nutrient absorption
items.content: Fats in cream help absorb fat‑soluble vitamins from other ingredients.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Cream and milk may cause discomfort for people who are lactose intolerant.

items.title: High fat content
items.content: Traditional white sauce contains a lot of saturated fat, so it should be consumed in moderation.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to dairy should avoid the sauce.

items.title: Salt and sodium
items.content: Gravy made from stock can be high in sodium; salt levels should be controlled.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Béchamel works well in casseroles, pasta, vegetable dishes and fish. Gravy is used as a sauce for meat, potatoes, dumplings and in soups. The sauce can be thinned with milk or stock, and flavored with cheese, herbs, or spices to taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared sauce in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. When frozen, it may separate; re‑mix thoroughly and gently reheat before use.
